source_text: Secundum hanc formam subiungimus: FIAT UOLUNTAS TUA IN CAEIIIS ET IN TERRA, non quod aliquis obsistat, quo minus uoluntas dei fiat, et ei successum uoluntatis suae oremus, sed in omnibus petimus fieri uoluntatem eius. ex interpretatione enim figurata carnis et spiritus nos sumus caelum et terra. quamquam etsi simpliciter intellegendum est, idem tamen est sensus petitionis, ut in nobis fiat uoluntas dei in terris, ut possit scilicet fieri et in caelis. quid autem deus uult quam incedere nos secundum suam disciplinam? petimus ergo substantiam et facultatem uoluntatis suae subministret nobis, ut salui simus et in caelis et in terris, quia summa est uoluntatis eius salus eorum quos adoptauit. est et illa dei uoluntas, quam dominus administrauit praedicando operando sustinendo. si enim ipse pronuntiauit non suam, sed patris facere se uoluntatem, sine dubio, quae faciebat, ea erat uoluntas patris, ad quae nunc nos uelut ad exemplaria prouocamur, ut et praedicemus et operemur et sustineamus ad mortem usque. quae ut implere possimus, opus est dei uoluntate. item dicentes, fiat uoluntas tua, uel eo nobis bene optamus, quod nihil mali sit in dei uoluntate, etiam si quid pro meritis cuiusque secus inrogatur. iam hoc dicto ad sufferentiam nosmetipsos praemonemus. dominus quoque cum sub instantiam passionis infirmitatem carnis demonstrare iam in sua carne uoluisset, pater, inquit, transfer poculum istud, et recordatus, nisi quod mea non, sed tua fiat uoluntas. ipse erat uoluntas et potestas patris et tamen ad demonstrationem sufferentiae debitae uoluntati se patris tradidit.
thought_title: God's will in heaven and on earth
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the third petition of the Lord's Prayer, after having treated the hallowing of God's name.
pass_a_gloss: According to this form we add: YOUR WILL BE DONE IN HEAVEN AND ON EARTH, not because anyone resists, so that the will of God may not be done, and we pray for him the success of his will, but in all things we ask that his will be done. For by the figurative interpretation of flesh and spirit we are heaven and earth. Although even if it is to be understood simply, nevertheless the sense of the petition is the same, that in us the will of God may be done on earth, so that it may be able, of course, to be done also in heaven. But what does God will except that we walk according to his teaching? Therefore we ask that he supply us the substance and power of his will, so that we may be saved both in heaven and on earth, because the sum of his will is the salvation of those whom he has adopted. There is also that will of God, which the Lord carried out by preaching, by working, by enduring. For if he himself declared that he did not his own will but the Father's, without doubt, the things which he was doing, those were the will of the Father, to which things we are now summoned as to examples, so that we also may preach and work and endure even to death. So that we may be able to fulfill these things, there is need of the will of God. Likewise, saying, your will be done, we wish well for ourselves even in this, that there is nothing evil in the will of God, even if something is inflicted on each person otherwise according to his merits. Already by this saying we warn ourselves beforehand toward endurance. The Lord also, when under the approach of his passion he had wished to show the weakness of the flesh already in his own flesh, said, Father, remove this cup, and he remembered, except that not mine, but your will be done. He himself was the will and power of the Father, and yet for the demonstration of the endurance owed to the will he handed himself over to the Father's will.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'teaching' for disciplina, not 'discipline'.
Substantia means the actual reality or being of God's will, facultas the ability or capacity to carry it out; kept literal to preserve the double request.

choices.english: we are summoned as to examples
choices.why: Prouocamur has the force of being called or challenged toward something; 'summoned' keeps the active call, and exemplaria as 'examples' preserves the plural pattern.
Sufferentia here is the capacity to bear suffering; 'endurance' is the plain English equivalent and avoids the narrower modern sense of 'suffering'.
Transfero means to carry across or take away; 'remove' is the natural English for the petition, and 'cup' matches the biblical image.

bible_refs.note: pater, transfer poculum istud, et recordatus, nisi quod mea non, sed tua fiat uoluntas

pass_b_english: Following this pattern we add: “Your will be done in heaven and on earth.” We do not say this because someone is resisting so that God’s will cannot be done, and we pray for the success of his will. Rather, we ask that his will be done in all things. For in the figurative interpretation of flesh and spirit, we ourselves are heaven and earth. Yet even if it must be understood simply, the sense of the petition is still the same: that God’s will be done in us on earth, so that it may also be done in heaven. What does God will except that we walk according to his teaching? We ask, then, that he supply us with the substance and power of his will, so that we may be saved both in heaven and on earth, because the highest point of his will is the salvation of those whom he has adopted.

There is also that will of God which the Lord carried out by preaching, by working, and by enduring. For if he himself declared that he did not his own will but the Father’s, then without doubt the things he was doing were the Father’s will. To these things we are now summoned as to examples, so that we too may preach and work and endure even to death. To be able to fulfill these things, we need the will of God. Likewise, when we say, “Your will be done,” we are wishing ourselves well in this too: that there is nothing evil in God’s will, even if something is inflicted on each person otherwise according to their deserts. By this saying we also warn ourselves beforehand toward endurance. The Lord too, when under the pressure of his passion he wished to show the weakness of the flesh already in his own flesh, said, “Father, remove this cup,” and then remembered, “Yet not my will, but that your will be done.” He himself was the will and power of the Father, and yet he handed himself over to the Father’s will to demonstrate the endurance that is owed.

problems.quote: and then remembered, “Yet not what I will, but what you will be done”
problems.source_quote: et recordatus, nisi quod mea non, sed tua fiat uoluntas
problems.why: Latin says “but that your will be done,” not “what you will be done,” changing the petition’s meaning.
problems.fix: and then recalled, “Not my will, but that your will be done.”
problems.ruling: Latin 'tua fiat uoluntas' = 'your will be done,' not 'what you will be done.' Translator conflates with Mt 26:39 wording, altering the petition's meaning.

edits.old: and then remembered, “Yet not what I will, but what you will be done”
edits.new: and then remembered, “Yet not my will, but that your will be done”

fixed: Corrected the quotation: source 'nisi quod mea non, sed tua fiat uoluntas' means 'except that not mine, but your will be done,' so the English now reads 'Yet not my will, but that your will be done.'

problems.why: The source does not cite a scripture reference here; the citation is an unwarranted addition.
problems.ruling: Source has no scripture reference; adding '(Matthew 26:39)' misleads reader into thinking it's in the Latin.

edits.old: said, “Father, remove this cup,” and then remembered, “Yet not my will, but that your will be done” (Matthew 26:39).
edits.new: said, “Father, remove this cup,” and then remembered, “Yet not my will, but that your will be done.”

problems.fix: and pray for the success of his will
problems.ruling: Source 'et ei successum uoluntatis suae oremus' = 'and we pray for the success of his will', English adds negation 'nor do we'
